## Lesson Content

### Lesson_Cassie_BeyondTheBreakroom- Lesson.docx

Workplace Edge – Lesson

Author: Cassie Savoie

**Lesson Overview**

**Lesson Title:** Beyond the Breakroom

**Pathway:** WE

**Audience:** multicultural teams (hybrid)

**Skill Focus:** making interpersonal connections and building trust

**Workplace Challenge:** A common workplace challenge is building trust amongst teammates and fostering a strong team connection. Effective communication and collaboration cannot happen without trust and interpersonal connection. If we don’t feel connected to our teammates, communication breaks down, trust is slow to build, and we don’t have a sense of belonging on the team.

**Building a strong team connection leads to trusting your teammates, and teammates who trust each other are more satisfied at work and produce better results. **

*(SLIDE 1)Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “Hello Learner! Welcome to the Beyond the Breakroom lesson. This lesson covers the topic of interpersonal team connections and how to build trust with your teammates. Don’t forget to check out the downloadable content. Happy learning!”*

*Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “Learners, while you go over the concepts and content in this lesson, you will be able to:*

**Lesson Objectives**

Learners will be able to:

- Reflect on their own experience interacting socially with their teammates.
- Write casual conversation starters relevant to their workplace context.
- Write a list of personal details they feel comfortable disclosing to teammates in social interactions.
- Apply the 3 simple steps to building team connection and practice the dos and don’ts of workplace social interactions.

**SPARK – Social Interactions at Work **

**Task: Personal Reflection **

*(SLIDE 2) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “First, let’s SPARK your interest in this topic while you reflect on your Social Interactions at Work. In the article, “Developing team trust: Leader insights for virtual settings”, Julie V. Dinh et al. (2021) claims:*

“Trust typically develops over time, through repeated positive interactions. Minor interactions, facilitated by physical proximity, can often accelerate this process. For example, the “water cooler gossip” that occurs in break rooms is often an unplanned but impactful way to gather colleagues and create affective bonds. In an in-person office setting, coworkers can stop by one another’s spaces to socialize informally and develop rapport. These opportunities for informal engagement are lost when you remove the physical environment. If left unchecked, a lack of interaction can lead to isolation and various undesirable effects: impacting trust, accelerating burnout, impairing senses of belongingness, et cetera (p. 3, para. 2).”

*Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “Workplace interactions are a crucial aspect of workplace belonging and fostering a strong sense of trust among teammates. These interactions can happen in person or online. As claimed in the quote above by Julie V. Dinh et al., fostering connections in person can sometimes be easier than fostering them while working online. Develop your ****self-awareness**** and ****social awareness**** skills by thinking back to a time when you had a casual interaction with a teammate (in person or online). Use the question prompts provided below to guide your reflection.” *

*PRO TIP: Set yourself up for success by writing your lesson reflections and activity responses in the downloadable Reflection Journal & Activity Log. You can refer back to your notes later on in the lesson.*

**Learner Instructions: **

1. Take 2-3 minutes to think back to a time when you had a casual interaction with a teammate at work.
2. Use the question prompts below to guide your reflection.
3. Take notes in your Reflection Journal, as you will refer back to them later in the lesson.

**Reflection Question Prompts:**

- Were you in person or online?
- Who initiated the conversation? You or them?
- What did you speak about?
- Did you learn anything about your teammate? If no, why not?
- Did you disclose anything about yourself during the conversation? If no, why not?
- How did you feel at the end of the conversation?

*(SLIDE 3) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “We typically spend one third of our lives at work, which means we are going to inevitably have lot of opportunity for social interactions with our teammates. Having casual conversations at work can sometimes be a bit awkward and may feel superficial if they don’t go well. This is especially true if you work on an intercultural team. *

*However, the more you develop interpersonal connections with your teammates, the better you will be able to communicate with them, which will lead to trusting them, empathizing with them, and finding ways to support one another when needed. Strengthening your ****self-awareness**** and your ****social awareness**** during these interactions will help you build stronger relationships and make better interpersonal connections.”*

**SHIFT – Casual Conversation Starters & Self-Disclosure**

<a id="_heading=h.l8g0ewntekac"></a>Blog Article: ‘The Pathway to Teams That Trust Each Other’

Language Focus: casual conversation starters

**Task Part 1: Reading + Reflection  **

Adding to the development of your ****self-awareness**** and ****social awareness**** skills, you also want to work towards further developing your ****relationship building skills****. Read the blog article, ‘The Pathway to Teams That Trust Each Other’ and answer the questions below.”*

<a id="_heading=h.b2eoxse4ux5p"></a>*PRO TIP: Check out the glossary of terms at the end of the blog article for definitions and example sentences of the vocabulary used in the article. *

<a id="_heading=h.6tbmva4fi945"></a>**Learner Instructions:**

1. Read the blog article, The Pathway to Teams That Trust Each Other’.
2. Take notes of any key ideas.
3. Answer the reflection questions below.

*(SLIDE 5) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “Now that you have finished reading the article, consider the reference to the McKinsey & Company research from 2024, which indicated that trust is a key factor in team efficiency and producing results. Thinking back to what you’ve read, answer the reflection questions below.”*

<a id="_heading=h.ecuncpqdwro1"></a>**Article Reflection Questions:**

1. In your opinion, why do you think trusting your teammates plays such a big role in team efficiency and producing better results?
2. The article recommends that you make *building a strong team connection* one of your main KPIs. Do you agree or disagree with this recommendation? Why?

*(SLIDE 6) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “The research from McKinsey & Company shows clear indicators of how companies with a high level of trust produce better results and are more efficient. The blog article states that trust is needed to have better communication and collaboration, so without trust, these other crucial workplace skills become more challenging. Teams who do not trust each other may not be able to work well together and may end up feeling dissatisfied at work as a result. For example, if you trust your teammate, you feel comfortable sharing information with them, and you can speak honestly to them about the progress on a project, the support required, and the hustle needed to get the work done efficiently. Without that trust, relying on teammates might not be possible.”*

*Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “In Abby Lewis’ (n.d.) HBR article, “Good leadership? It all starts with trust.”, she summarizes Paul J. Zak’s (2017) HBR study, “The Neuroscience of Trust”:*

“According to a study in Harvard Business Review, people at high-trust companies report **74% less stress, 106% more energy at work, 50% higher productivity, 13% fewer sick days, 76% more engagement, 29% more satisfaction with their lives, and 40% less burnout** than people at low-trust companies (para. 4).”

*Intercultural Perspective: Trust is a deep cultural attitude that may vary greatly from culture to culture. In some cultures, trust may only be built based on knowing the quality or level of a person’s performance, achievements, or qualifications, whereas in other cultures, trust is built over time through interactions and getting to know someone and may not be connected to their level of knowledge or professional achievements. Working on an intercultural team means that trust may be slower to develop based on team dynamics and cultural expectations of how trust is earned. From Richard Barrett’s (2019) perspective, trust is made up of 2 components: Character and Competence. His Trust Matrix categorizes Intent and Integrity under Character and Capability and Results under Competence (Barrett, 2019). To learn more, read his article here!   *

AI-generated content may be incorrect.](data:image/png;base64,)*
(Barrett, 2019)*

**Task Part 2: Write Casual Conversation Starters**

*(SLIDE 7) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “The way you get beyond the breakroom and take the pathway to building trust is engaging in casual interactions/conversations with your teammates. These interactions are where you can get to know your teammates better and where you have the opportunity to disclose a little about yourself as well. It is also where you get to further develop your ****relationship skills****.”*

*“Remember the 3 simple steps to building a stronger team connection.”  *

<a id="_heading=h.59l7028o380q"></a>**3 Simple Steps to Building Stronger Team Connections:**

1. Use casual conversation openers and a “get to know you better” attitude to start discussions with your teammates to begin making connections.
2. Build trust by offering small self-disclosures in return. A little self-disclosure goes a long way.
3. Strengthen the connection and trust by showing that you care enough to remember what you talked about. Make a note to follow-up later.

*(SLIDE 8) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “To get you started with these 3 simple steps, look at the examples of ****casual conversation starters**** below that you could use in the workplace.”*

*Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “It’s important to remember that context is key! Interpersonal relationships are built over time and understanding the context of the team (E.g., how long have you been teammates, what project are you currently working on), the team or workplace culture that already exists (E.g., what are the current team dynamics like, how often do you and your teammates get to interact outside of work project discussions), and the backgrounds and experiences that your teammates bring to the team dynamics is important to consider. Your own cultural background and experiences also play a role in these interactions.”*

<a id="_heading=h.u42d6tb1ik8w"></a>**Example Casual Conversation Starters:**

- How’s your day going so far?
- What’s something good that happened this week?
- I saw your project update; could you tell me more about that?
- How’s the project feeling on your end?

*(SLIDE 9) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “Think about your current team dynamics and workplace context. Think about the interpersonal connections you may or may not already have. If building connections and trust with your teammates is a key KPI, what are some casual conversation openers that might be relevant for your workplace context? Label each conversation starter with the potential audience you would use it with. For example, if the question is appropriate for chatting with a new teammate who just joined, or if the question is better suited for chatting with your boss.”*

<a id="_heading=h.6kyaap96j8so"></a>**Learner Instructions: **

1. Think about your workplace context.
2. <a id="_heading=h.snw9iln4kgze"></a>Go to your Activity Log and make a list of at least 3 additional questions or conversation starters that would be applicable in your workplace context.
3. Label questions with the audience you would use these questions with.

**Casual Conversation Starter**

**Audience**

How’s your day going so far?

Anyone on the team

I saw your project update; could you tell me more about that?

Supervisor, teammate on another project

*(SLIDE10) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “Okay, now you have some casual conversation starters to take away with you to use in your own workplace. As you get more comfortable having these conversations, you can add more options to your list. Check out this article from Jennifer Herrity (2025) on Indeed, where she lists out 150 conversation starters ranging from, casual to deep and covering situational contexts such as employee gatherings, interviews, and networking events.”*

**Task Part 3: Write a List for Self-Disclosure **

*(SLIDE 11) “The next simple step to prepare for is ****self-disclosure****. Take a look at the example self-disclosures below."*

*“Self-disclosure can sometimes be tricky for some people based on their previous experience, their cultural background, or the culture of their organization. When you think about what you feel comfortable disclosing, your emotional safety is essential. To get you started, you may want to consider broader categories such as interests, hobbies, family, previous experience, travel, food, cultural celebrations, etc., or anything else you feel psychologically safe enough to share or speak about at work. Your main goal is to build stronger connections with your team and develop your relationship skills. From there, once you have started to establish more trust, you could think about a second level of appropriate self-disclosure to help deepen your relationship building.”*

*PRO TIP: Remember, a little disclosure goes a long way in building trust but do it within your comfort zone.*

<a id="_heading=h.o1iwd2q5xdql"></a>**Example Self-Disclosures:**

**General Self-Disclosure**

**Second Level of Self-Disclosure**

I really like to [insert an activity you like doing].

*Example: I really like to travel.*

Share more details about the activity.

- I’ve been to [insert #] countries.
- My favourite country was [insert country].
- While travelling in [insert country], [insert personal story about something that happened while travelling].

*Example: I’ve been to 10 countries, but Italy was my favourite. While I was travelling there, I got to see really great sites, eat lots of delicious food, and attend the wedding of a friend. *

I’ve lived in [insert city] for [insert length of time there].

*Example: I’ve lived in Vancouver for 10 years. *

I moved to [insert city] from [insert city you came from].

*Example: I moved to Vancouver 10 years ago from Seoul, South Korea.*

*(SLIDE 12) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “Preparing for self-disclosure can help you avoid awkward interactions with your teammates and increase your emotional safety. Sometimes, you can get caught off guard when someone asks you a personal question, or you might not feel comfortable with self-disclosure at work. The more prepared you are, the more easily you will be able to handle the situation and build your confidence. Take some time to write out a list of topics you feel comfortable disclosing at work.”*

(SLIDE 13) **Learner Instructions: **

1. Think about your own hobbies, interests, what you like to read, places you’ve been, food you like, or cultural traditions in your family.
2. Go to your Activity Log and make a list of topics you feel comfortable speaking about at work during a social interaction.
3. Make a second list of specific things within those topics.

*(SLIDE 14) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “Okay, now you have some great topics for self-disclosure. Once you’ve practiced using these in the workplace, you can update your list with new topics or add more detail to the existing topics. As you get more comfortable, you can also let the self-disclosure come naturally during an interaction.” *

*Intercultural Perspective: Self-disclosure norms vary from culture to culture. Some people from low-context cultures may feel more comfortable disclosing information about themselves at work, whereas people from high-context cultures may not feel as comfortable with this. Communicating across cultures can feel daunting! That’s okay. If you are curious and want to learn more about either self-disclosure or communicating across cultures, check out these extra resources:*

*Self-Disclosure (Khan, 2024) *

*Cultural Communication (Farmer, 2025)*

<a id="_heading=h.3l4wzeo2g8h0"></a>**STRETCH –** **Building Strong Team Connections in the Real World **

**Application Task:** Apply the 3 simple steps in the workplace.

**Task Part 1: DO and DON’T Statements **

*(SLIDE 15) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “You’ve SHIFTED your perspective, so now it’s time to STRETCH your abilities and apply these concepts in your workplace. Now that you’ve prepared casual conversation starters and a list of personal details you could disclose at work, let’s go over important DOs and DON’Ts of these essential social interactions.”*

**Learner Instructions: **

1. Read the statements on each card.
2. Drag and drop each statement into the correct category: DO or DON’T.
3. Take a moment to reflect on each list and how it will apply to your real-world conversations.

<a id="_heading=h.nvkxoxlmeko0"></a>**DOS & DON’TS for Social Interactions & Self-Disclosure (Adapted from HBR podcast – Bates, 2024**)

![Checkmark with solid fill](data:image/png;base64,)DO

- Share small details about yourself (within your comfort zone) – hobbies, interests, travel, food, and even cultural practices can be fun topics for easy discussion
- Ask questions with curiosity and a “get to know you better” attitude
- Listen actively
- Respond with genuine interest
- Respect other people’s cultural backgrounds and experiences
- Share true details about yourself

![Close with solid fill](data:image/png;base64,)DON’T

- Overshare too many personal details / too much information (TMI) can make people feel awkward and uncomfortable, and it can be a conversation stopper
- Talk about yourself the whole time
- Interrupt or talk over people
- Make rude or insensitive comments
- Stereotype or judge people based on information they choose to share or disclose
- Overexaggerate or share fake details

**Task Part 2: Workplace Conversation Scenario **

*(SLIDE 16) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “With the DOs and DON’Ts in your mind, you have all the tools ready to apply your learning in the workplace. Start small, disclose a little about yourself, and make a note to follow up with that person later. This not only shows that you were ****listening actively****, but it also shows that you have ****empathy**** for your teammates. **Task Part 3: Workplace Interaction Journal & Continued Reflection**

*(SLIDE 18) Articulate Instructor Audio/Speech Bubble: “Applying these lessons in your workplace interactions is a great way to enhance your learning. However, taking time to reflect on each interaction, assessing your emotions and your progress, as well as making small adjustments over time, and then reflecting again will help to consolidate the lesson take-aways and turn it into noticeable behavioural changes. You are working towards a strong sense of self-awareness, which will help you strengthen your social awareness and relationship skills in the workplace.*

*Each time you have a social interaction at work, give yourself space and time afterwards to reflect on the interaction, take notes about what went well, what needs improvement, and how you want to approach the interaction the next time. Come back to this lesson each time to refresh your memory on the important learning you’ve gained.”*

<a id="_heading=h.71mqr747j33a"></a>**Learner Instructions Part 1: **

1. After each social interaction at work, make a brief note in your journal about what you talked about. Also, take note of a follow-up question you could ask.
2. When you see that person again, ask them a follow-up question based on what you talked about in the initial interaction.
3. Repeat this with each interaction leaving yourself weekly space and time to reflect and update your list of conversation starters and disclosure topics.

**Learner Instructions Part 2:**

1. After you’ve had 3-5 social interactions at work, take time to reflect on the interactions.
2. Use the questions prompts below to guide your reflection.
3. Go back to your notes from the first reflection activity at the beginning of this lesson.
	1. How does that interaction/story compare with your most recent interactions after applying the concepts from this lesson?
	2. What improvements have you noticed?

**Reflection Question Prompts:**

- Were you in person or online?
- Who initiated the conversation? You or them?
- What did you speak about?
- Did you learn anything about your teammate? If no, why not?
- What did you disclose about yourself in the conversation?
- How did you feel at the end of the conversation?
- Did you ask the person a follow-up question the next time you saw them? If no, why not?
- What would you do differently next time?

## Scenarios

### Beyond the Breakroom Branching Scenario.pdf

“Beyond the Breakroom” Branching Scenario

1) Scenario Charter
Lesson Title: Beyond the Breakroom.

Problem Statement (from the lesson’s Workplace Challenge)​
A common workplace challenge is building trust amongst teammates and fostering a strong team
connection. Without interpersonal connection, effective communication and collaboration cannot
happen. When teammates don’t feel connected, communication breaks down, trust is slow to build,
and we lose a sense of belonging—a challenge amplified in hybrid settings where spontaneous
“water‑cooler” interactions are reduced.

Learning Objectives (verbatim from the lesson)​
Learners will be able to:

    1.​ Reflect on their own experience interacting socially with their teammates.
    2.​ Write casual conversation starters relevant to their workplace context.
    3.​ Write a list of personal details they feel comfortable disclosing to teammates in social
        interactions.
    4.​ Apply the 3 simple steps to building team connection and practice the dos and don’ts of
        workplace social interactions.

Intended Skills

    ●​ Self‑awareness
    ●​ Social awareness
    ●​ Relationship‑building skills

Framework​
SPARK → SHIFT → STRETCH (awareness → language/perspective shift → real‑world application).

3 Simple Steps to Building Team Connection (from the lesson)

    1.​ Open — Use casual conversation openers to initiate connection.
    2.​ Disclose — Offer small, appropriate self‑disclosures within your comfort zone.
    3.​ Follow‑up — Show you remember; check back later to strengthen trust.

Success Signals (observable behaviors | used as subtle badges on screen)

    ●​ OPEN: Uses a context‑appropriate casual conversation starter.
    ●​ DISCLOSE: Shares a small, appropriate personal detail within comfort/safety.
    ●​ FOLLOW‑UP: Remembers and checks back later to show care.
   ●​ DOs behaviors: Listen actively, respond with genuine interest, respect cultural
      backgrounds; avoids DON’Ts (oversharing, dominating, interrupting, insensitive comments,
      stereotyping, exaggeration).

Context, Characters & What Happens (narrative spine)

   ●​ Setting: Global, multicultural team working hybrid (in‑person + online). Focus: recreating
      informal engagement lost online (the “water‑cooler” effect).
   ●​ Protagonist: You, the Learner (addressed in second person).
   ●​ Colleagues: Rina (primary), Mateo (optional), representing diverse regions/accents.
   ●​ Narrative arc: In the week leading up to a cross‑regional feature demo, you navigate
      three everyday touchpoints—virtual lobby, post‑meeting chat, and later follow‑up—to
      rebuild trust using Open → Disclose → Follow‑up, with DOs/DON’Ts and intercultural
      notes guiding micro‑choices. Research flashes (Dinh 2021; McKinsey 2024; Zak 2017)
      appear briefly as lower‑thirds.

Research beats to visualize

   ●​ Dinh et al. (2021): Informal proximity‑based interactions accelerate trust; removing the
      physical environment removes unplanned engagement and can lead to isolation and
      weakened belonging.
   ●​ McKinsey (2024): Trust is a key factor in team efficiency and results.
   ●​ Zak (HBR, 2017): High‑trust orgs report less stress, more energy, higher productivity,
      fewer sick days, more engagement, higher life satisfaction, and less burnout.

Logline​
A multicultural hybrid team member learns how intentional micro‑interactions—opening, small
self‑disclosures, and following up—rebuild trust and connection when “water‑cooler” moments are
missing.

2) Branching Structure (A/B/C) — Narrative Decisions with
Consequence & Coaching
      Important: Consequences play in scene (dialogue + reactions). Feedback appears as
      coaching reflections (no “correct/incorrect” labels). Badges (OPEN / DISCLOSE /
      FOLLOW‑UP / DOs) pulse unobtrusively to signal observable behaviors.

Here’s the branching structure (A/B/C) exactly as set for the narrative storyboard—three decisions,
each with options, in‑scene consequences, and a short coaching note.
    Situational Setup → Decision 1 (OPEN)
Context: Virtual standup lobby (morning). You and Rina join a minute early—tiny window to replace
lost “water‑cooler” moments.

Prompt: What do you say to start connection?

    ●​ A — “How’s your day going so far?”​
       Consequence: Warm, low‑stakes opening; rapport breathes; culturally safe.​
       Coaching: Small openers help recreate informal touchpoints; rotate the approved starter list.
    ●​ B — “Did you finish that report yet?”​
       Consequence: Transactional tone; rapport skipped.​
       Coaching: Add a brief human opener first; hybrid teams need intentional micro‑connections.
    ●​ C — (Stay silent)​
       Consequence: Awkward pause; missed micro‑moment; distance grows.​
       Coaching: Silence reduces informal engagement; pick one safe starter to keep handy.

    Situational Shift → Decision 2 (DISCLOSE)
Context: After the meeting. Rina mentions cooking with family—chance for small, safe reciprocity.

Prompt: How do you respond to build trust?

    ●​ A — “Nice! I love cooking too… What did you make?”​
       Consequence: Balanced sharing; curiosity; food/hobbies broadly safe.​
       Coaching: A little disclosure goes a long way—prepare a short “safe topics” list in advance.
    ●​ B — “Cool. I’ve travelled to 10 countries…” (long monologue)​
       Consequence: Self‑focused; oversharing risk; rapport stalls.​
       Coaching: Trim to one brief detail and ask one question back; avoid DON’Ts.
    ●​ C — “I don’t really talk about personal stuff at work.”​
       Consequence: No reciprocity; connection cools.​
       Coaching: Pre‑plan 3 safe topics (e.g., food, hobbies, places lived) to prevent awkwardness.

    Situational Shift → Decision 3 (FOLLOW‑UP)
Context: Later in the week (team chat). The demo is tomorrow; a thoughtful follow‑up can cement
trust loops.

Prompt: How do you show you remember and care?
   ●​ A — “Hey—how did that dish turn out the other day?”​
      Consequence: Specific memory + care; rapport deepens.​
      Coaching: Remembering & checking back strengthens trust over time.
   ●​ B — “Hope your week’s going okay.”​
      Consequence: Polite; doesn’t deepen connection.​
      Coaching: Add one remembered detail to make it relational, not generic.
   ●​ C — “I need help with my project—free now?”​
      Consequence: Transactional; warmth drops.​
      Coaching: Lead with relationship first; then make the request.

   Badges (on‑screen signals)

   ●​ OPEN (Step 1), DISCLOSE (Step 2), FOLLOW‑UP (Step 3), DOs (active listening, genuine
      interest, respect).​
      These pulse unobtrusively during the scene to signal the behavior shown—no “grading”
      labels on screen.

Slide 1 — Decision Point 1: OPEN
Scene header: Virtual meeting waiting room, Monday morning.​
Ambient: Calendar pings, keyboards, quiet office bed.

Action & Dialogue (watch first):

   ●​ You (joining early; camera on): “Morning.”
   ●​ Sarah (pops in, adjusts headset): “Hey—good morning.”​
      (Tiny beat—the moment you’d normally lose online.)

Prompt on screen:​
What do you say to start a casual, low‑pressure connection? (Step 1: OPEN)
Options (buttons):​
A. “How’s your day going so far?” (conversation starter from the lesson)​
B. “Did you finish that report yet?”​
C. (You stay silent and check your email.)

Slide 1A — You choose A. (★ BEST)

Play scene:

   ●​ You: “Hey, Sarah—how’s your day going so far?”
   ●​ Sarah (shoulders drop slightly): “Pretty good—early start with the APAC team. You?”

                             ✅          ✅
   ●​ You: “Doing alright—coffee’s helping.” (shared smile)​
      Badge pulse: OPEN        • DOs      (curiosity, genuine interest)

Cut-in coaching (2‑3 lines, not a grade):

   ●​ Why this helps: A simple opener replaces that lost informal beat and invites rapport in hybrid.
   ●​ Try next time: Rotate your starters—“What’s something good that happened this week?” or
      “How’s the project feeling on your end?” (Slide 8)

Navigation: Continue → Slide 2

Slide 1B — You choose B. (◇ NEUTRAL)

Play scene:

   ●​ You: “Hey—did you finish that report yet?”
   ●​ Sarah: “Almost there—I’ll share after the standup.” (tone flattens; micro‑hesitation)​
      Badge pulse: OPEN ⚠ (transactional)

Cut-in coaching:

   ●​ What’s the risk: You skipped rapport; in hybrid, we have to create those micro‑connections
      on purpose.
   ●​ Quick fix: One line of human check‑in before the task helps trust form.

Navigation: Continue → Slide 2

Slide 1C — You choose C. (✕ INCORRECT)
Play scene:

                       ⛔
   ●​ (You glance down at email; Sarah checks her chat. The moment passes.)​
      Badge: OPEN      (missed moment)

Cut-in coaching:

   ●​ Why it hurts: Silence means the informal touchpoint disappears; that can increase distance
      and slow trust.
   ●​ Try next time: Keep one safe starter ready—“How’s your day going so far?”

Navigation: Continue → Slide 2

Slide 2 — Decision Point 2: DISCLOSE
Scene header: Right after the standup. Video ends, both of you linger a moment.​
Ambient: Call disconnect chime; office background.

Action & Dialogue (watch first):

   ●​ Sarah (a little more relaxed now): “We tried a new family recipe this weekend.”
   ●​ You (smile; considering your response).

Prompt on screen:​
How do you respond to build trust with a small, appropriate self‑disclosure? (Step 2: DISCLOSE)

Options:​
A. “Nice! I love cooking too—especially trying recipes from different places. What did you
make?”​
B. “Cool—yeah, I’ve travelled to 10 countries and cooked amazing food everywhere…” (you
keep going)​
C. “I don’t really talk about personal stuff at work.”

Slide 2A — You choose A. (★ BEST)

Play scene:

   ●​ You: “Nice—I love cooking too—especially trying recipes from different places. What did
      you make?”
   ●​ Sarah (lights up): “Dumplings—my grandmother’s recipe! We finally got the folds right.”

                              ✅          ✅
   ●​ You: “That’s awesome—sounds like a win.”​
      Badges: DISCLOSE         • DOs   (genuine interest, active listening)

Cut-in coaching:

   ●​ Why this helps: A little disclosure + curiosity creates reciprocity and safety.
   ●​ Prep list: Food, hobbies, travel, cultural celebrations, places lived—with one second‑level
      detail each. (Slides 11–14)

Navigation: Continue → Slide 3

Slide 2B — You choose B. (◇ NEUTRAL)

Play scene:

   ●​ You: “Cool—yeah, I’ve travelled to 10 countries and cooked amazing food everywhere.
      The best was—” (you keep talking)
   ●​ Sarah (polite smile, glances aside): “Wow—sounds incredible.” (energy drops a touch)​
      Badge: DISCLOSE ⚠ (dominates space)

Cut-in coaching:

   ●​ Risk: It’s still disclosure, but it tilts self‑focused—can feel like oversharing.
   ●​ Try: Share one small detail, then ask one question back.

Navigation: Continue → Slide 3

Slide 2C — You choose C. (✕ INCORRECT)

Play scene:

   ●​ You: “I don’t really talk about personal stuff at work.”

                             ⛔
   ●​ Sarah: “Oh—okay.” (topic ends)​
      Badge: DISCLOSE          (no reciprocity)

Cut-in coaching:

   ●​ Why it hurts: Zero self‑disclosure removes the chance to build rapport.
   ●​ Low‑risk path: Use broader topics (food/hobbies) while staying in your comfort zone. (Slides
      11–14)

B. “Hope your week’s going okay.”​
C. “Hey, I need help with my project—free now?”

Slide 3A — You choose A. (★ BEST)

Play scene (chat bubbles):

                              ✅         ✅

Cut-in coaching:

   ●​ Why this helps: Remembering + checking back shows care and sustains trust.
   ●​ Habit: Make a quick note after a chat about one detail to revisit.

Slide 3B — You choose B. (◇ NEUTRAL)

Play scene:

      Badge: FOLLOW‑UP ⚠ (friendly but thin)

Slide 3C — You choose C. (✕ INCORRECT)

Slide 4 — Research & Intercultural Note (SHIFT/reflect)
On‑screen (short cards):

   ●​ Trust grows through repeated positive interactions; losing physical proximity removes
      unplanned engagement and can lead to isolation.
   ●​ Trust is a key factor in team efficiency and results.
   ●​ High‑trust workplaces: less stress, more energy, higher productivity, fewer sick days, more
      engagement, higher life satisfaction, less burnout.
   ●​ Intercultural lens: Some teams build trust via interactions/character; others via
      competence/results. Comfort with self‑disclosure varies—start broad and pace depth.​
      (All language condensed from the lesson slides and summaries.)

Navigation: Continue → Slide 5 (Conclusion)

Slide 5 — Conclusion (STRETCH)
Checklist (from the lesson):

   ●​ Open with a casual starter (e.g., “How’s your day going so far?”).
   ●​ Disclose one small, safe detail—within your comfort zone (food, hobbies, travel, cultural
      celebrations, places lived).
   ●​ Follow‑up later to show you remember and care.
   ●​ Practice DOs; avoid DON’Ts (listen actively, respond with interest, respect backgrounds;
      avoid oversharing, dominating, interrupting, insensitive comments, stereotyping,
      exaggeration).

Reflection prompts (Slides 2, 10, 18):

   ●​ Were you in person or online? Who initiated? What did you speak about? What did you
      disclose? How did you feel? Did you follow up? What will you do differently next time?

Final VO:​
“Connection grows through small, genuine moments—one conversation at a time.”

6) SCORM Variables + Scoring Logic (kept under the hood;
experience stays narrative)
      Implementation: Use a Storyline 360 interactive‑video block inside Rise 360 for
      variables/scoring/SCORM. UI shows badges + coaching, not grades. (Scoring per
      your spec: A=10, B=5, C=0; Pass=20/30.)

Variables (Storyline):

   ●​ decision1_choice (Text: “A”/“B”/“C”)
   ●​ decision2_choice (Text: “A”/“B”/“C”)
   ●​ decision3_choice (Text: “A”/“B”/“C”)
   ●​ total_score (Number; default 0)

Scoring:

   ●​ A = 10, B = 5, C = 0 → max = 30.
   ●​ Passing Score: ≥ 20/30.

Plain‑English Logic:
         ●​ On each decision, set decisionX_choice and add 10/5/0 to total_score.
         ●​ On the final summary, if all three decisions are set and total_score ≥ 20, report
            Passed/Completed; else Completed/Failed or keep Incomplete per LMS policy.

JSON‑like contract (for devs)

{
    "variables": {
​           "decision1_choice": {"type":"string","values":["A","B","C"],"default":""},
​           "decision2_choice": {"type":"string","values":["A","B","C"],"default":""},
​           "decision3_choice": {"type":"string","values":["A","B","C"],"default":""},
​           "total_score": {"type":"number","min":0,"max":30,"default":0}
    },
    "scoring_rules": {"A":10, "B":5, "C":0},
    "pass_threshold": 20,
    "completion_logic": {
​           "all_decisions_made": true,
​           "passed_when": "total_score >= 20"
    },
    "reporting": {
​           "SCORM_1.2": {"score_raw":"cmi.core.score.raw","status":"cmi.core.lesson_status"},
​           "SCORM_2004":
{"score_raw":"cmi.score.raw","success":"cmi.success_status","completion":"cmi.completion_status"}
    },
    "suspend_data": ["decision1_choice","decision2_choice","decision3_choice","total_score"]
}

Completion Trigger

         ●​ SCORM 1.2: If all decisions set and total_score ≥ 20 → lesson_status="passed";
            else "failed" or "incomplete".
         ●​ SCORM 2004: If all decisions set and total_score ≥ 20 →
            success_status="passed", completion_status="completed".

Resume: Enabled (store variables in suspend data).

7) Developer Notes for Rise 360
Authoring Approach

   ●​ Build in Storyline 360 as an interactive‑video (decisions via time‑based hotspots; badges
      as layers; coaching panels after each scene beat). Embed in Rise as a Storyline block for
      SCORM. (Rise’s native scenario doesn’t expose custom scoring variables.)

Recommended Rise Flow

   1.​ Text/Image blocks: Intro + Workplace Challenge + brief research cards (Dinh, McKinsey,
       Zak).
   2.​ Storyline block: The narrative interactive video (decisions, badges, coaching).
   3.​ Knowledge‑check blocks (optional): Non‑scored recaps of DOs/DON’Ts and 3 Steps.
   4.​ Attachment blocks: Downloadables—Reflection Journal & Activity Log, Conversation
       Starter List, Self‑Disclosure Planning Worksheet (from Slides 2, 8, 11–14, 18).
   5.​ Accordion/Text blocks: 3 Simple Steps; DOs/DON’Ts quick reference.

Accessibility & Inclusion

   ●​ Open captions on all video; strong color contrast; keyboard‑navigable hotspots;
      descriptive alt text; downloadable transcript; globally accessible language (avoid idioms).

Visual/Audio Style

   ●​ Neutral brand palette; diverse casting/voices; ambient cues for micro‑beats (chat pings,
      cursor blinks); lower‑third research flashes (brief, non‑lecture).

SCORM Export

   ●​ Export SCORM 1.2 (or 2004 if your LMS prefers success/completion split). Track completion
      by Storyline results (total_score). Gate Rise progression with Continue block set to
      “Complete block above”.

References (as they should appear on a “Sources” card in Rise)

   ●​ Dinh, Julie V. et al. (2021). “Developing team trust: Leader insights for virtual settings.”
      (Quoted in lesson.)
   ●​ De Smet, Aaron et al. (2024). Go, teams: When teams get healthier, the whole organization
      benefits (McKinsey). (Summarized in lesson.)
   ●​ Zak, P. (2017). The Neuroscience of Trust (outcomes summarized via Abby Lewis’ HBR
      article in lesson).
